title: The moon can't be stolen
hook: the hermit Ryokan gives a thief his clothes and wishes he could give him the moon (Zen story, Japan)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Hakuin, who met blame and apology with the same three words: is that so. Your line was the child in front of you.

One room. A straw roof. A bowl, a cushion, a few poems written on scraps of paper. That was the hut of Ryokan, a Zen monk and poet who lived alone at the foot of a mountain in Japan. Tradition remembers him playing with the village children and begging for his rice, and his poems are still read today. One evening, while Ryokan is out walking, a thief slips into the hut, looking for something to steal. There is nothing. Then Ryokan comes home, and finds him.
screen: `ONE ROOM, A STRAW ROOF.` → `RYOKAN, MONK AND POET.` → `A THIEF IN THE EMPTY HUT.`

segments.voice: Ryokan isn't angry. He's sorry. You've come such a long way to visit me, he says, and you shouldn't go home empty-handed. Please, take my clothes. He takes off the robe he's wearing and hands it over. The thief, bewildered, grabs the clothes and runs off into the dark. Ryokan sits down, naked, in his doorway, and looks up. The moon is rising, huge and bright. And he says to himself: poor fellow. I wish I could have given him this beautiful moon. The story is usually tied to a short poem Japanese tradition credits to Ryokan: the thief left it behind, the moon in my window. Scholars can't say for sure the robbery happened just this way, but the poem and the story have traveled together for a long time. Now look at what Ryokan knows. The thief came for things. Ryokan barely had any, and gave away the last of them without a fight. What he treasured, the thief couldn't carry off, because it wasn't his to keep in the first place. The moon doesn't belong to anyone. It shines on the hut and the thief's road the same. Ryokan's wish is the whole teaching: he wants the thief to have what he himself has. Not the robe. The seeing. The quiet. A night bright enough to be rich in. Things can be guarded carefully, and still be lost. The moon stays.
screen: `TAKE MY CLOTHES.` · `I WISH I COULD GIVE HIM THE MOON.` · `THE THIEF LEFT IT BEHIND.` · `WHAT CAN'T BE CARRIED OFF.` · then, large: `THE MOON STAYS.`

segments.voice: Think of something you have that no one could steal, a view you love, a memory, a skill, the fact that you're breathing, and rest in it. Then think of one small thing you could give with nothing asked back: a coat you don't wear, your time, a kind word to someone who didn't earn it. Let it go already, in your mind, the way Ryokan let go of his robe.
Ryokan. A Zen monk and poet who gave a thief his clothes, and wished he could give him the moon too.
Your line: the moon stays. Ryokan never counted the robe as lost. That's day forty-six.

howItsDone: Ryokan is remembered in Japan as a poet-monk of simple living, and Zen teachers tell the story of the thief and the moon when talking about generosity and letting go of possessions.

notes: Ryokan (Ryōkan Taigu, 1758–1831), Sōtō Zen monk and poet, hut on Mount Kugami: described generally as 'around the year 1800' and 'at the foot of a mountain'. Confirm.
The poem usually given as 盗人に取り残されし窓の月 is paraphrased ('the thief left it behind, the moon in my window'), not quoted. Confirm the attribution to Ryokan and the paraphrase.
